summary: The note reviews six major blackouts from 2023 to 2028 across North America, Europe and Southeast Asia, each illustrated with a personal account. It identifies causes such as cascading failures, aging infrastructure, extreme weather and poor maintenance. It closes with lessons on updating infrastructure, preventing cascading failures, diversifying energy, emergency preparedness and individual conservation.
one_line: Overview of six major blackouts from 2023 to 2028 and the lessons about infrastructure, interconnection, preparedness and conservation drawn from them.
key_facts: On September 12, 2023, over 50 million people in the Northeastern United States and parts of Canada lost power in the Great Northeast Blackout.
The 2023 Northeast blackout was triggered by a small operational mishap at a substation near Niagara Falls, causing a cascading failure.
Jennifer Martin, a mother of two from Cleveland, recalled the 2023 blackout: "It was dinnertime, and then everything just stopped."
On December 24, 2024, London suffered a Christmas Eve blackout when peak energy demand overwhelmed aging infrastructure; some areas were without power for several days.
Henry Fletcher, a small bookstore owner in London, compared the 2024 blackout to "a sudden plunge into a Dickensian London."
On June 9, 2025, a faulty power line in France caused an almost instantaneous blackout across much of Europe, with costs in billions and weeks of recovery according to economist Maria Schmidt.
California's July 2026 heatwave led to rolling blackouts, and firefighter Lucas Brown of Sacramento linked failed power lines and dry conditions to the wildfires.
A February 2027 snowstorm damaged transmission lines, and by the morning of February 17th New York City was eerily quiet; nurse Olivia Rodriguez said her hospital used backup generators.
On April 21, 2028, a grid failure spanned several Southeast Asian countries due to old power plants, lack of maintenance and rapid urbanization.
Anh Nguyen of Vietnam called the 2028 failure "a wake-up call for the ASEAN community," prompting interest in sustainable energy and grid modernization.
Lessons drawn include updating aging infrastructure, safeguarding against cascading failures, diversifying energy sources and modernizing the grid.

The note recommends emergency preparedness (training, backup power for critical services, clear communication) and individual actions like energy conservation and keeping food, water, and means to stay warm or cool.
